title: Australia should do more to back Japan and the ICC in the face of US sanctions
gist: Simon Henderson argues Australia's 'quiet diplomacy' response to US sanctions on the International Criminal Court, including on its Japanese president Judge Tomoko Akane, has been underwhelming compared with Japan's escalating public pushback. He urges Canberra to publicly denounce the sanctions, coordinate with Japan, and block their implementation in Australia, including advising banks against overcompliance.

themes.theme: US sanctions campaign against the ICC

insights.claim: In August 2026 the US sanctioned ICC President Judge Tomoko Akane, a Japanese national, and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye.
insights.speaker: Simon Henderson
insights.so_what: US sanctions are reaching officials of allied nationality, widening compliance exposure for allied institutions.

insights.claim: When the first round of US sanctions against the ICC began in February 2025, Australia did not join 79 other countries in condemning the move.
insights.speaker: Simon Henderson
insights.so_what: Shows Australia's consistent reluctance to break publicly with Washington.
insights.locator: When the first round of US sanctions

insights.claim: ICC President Akane stated after the latest sanctions that the court's fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it.
insights.speaker: Simon Henderson
insights.so_what: The ICC's survival depends on member-state willingness to resist US financial pressure.
insights.quote: “Its fate now rests also in the hands of the States that created it.”
insights.locator: After the latest US sanctions were imposed

insights.claim: Neither Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese nor Foreign Minister Penny Wong has issued a statement on the US sanctions against the ICC, and Wong has declined to criticise the US directly.
insights.speaker: Simon Henderson
insights.so_what: Canberra is prioritising alliance management with Washington over public positioning.

insights.claim: Australia only belatedly joined a 9 October joint statement with Japan and other countries on the latest sanctions, and none of the Australian Embassy in Japan's social media accounts have referenced the sanctions or that statement.
insights.speaker: Simon Henderson
insights.so_what: Visible solidarity gaps can weigh on allied trust in the Australia-Japan relationship.
insights.locator: In response to the most recent round

insights.claim: Henderson argues Australia's response shows its 'elevated relationship' with Japan has limits when support risks confrontation with Washington, driven by concern about angering an unpredictable Trump administration.
insights.speaker: Simon Henderson
insights.so_what: Middle powers are self-censoring to avoid US retaliation, a signal of US coercive leverage over allies.

insights.claim: Australia's response to the US sanctions is a test of what its 'indispensable partnership' with Japan means in practice, 50 years after the NARA Treaty.
insights.speaker: Simon Henderson
insights.so_what: Bilateral partnership rhetoric may not translate into costly political support.
insights.quote: Australia’s response to the US sanctions is a test of what its “indispensable partnership” with Japan means in practice.

insights.claim: Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the US sanctions on the ICC are incompatible with Japan's position and raised the matter directly with President Donald Trump on 22 September despite US urging not to.
insights.speaker: Simon Henderson
insights.so_what: Japan is willing to openly challenge Washington on rule-of-law issues, a notable shift in a core US ally.

insights.claim: Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi outlined Japan's views on the sanctions in a 10 October call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
insights.speaker: Simon Henderson
insights.so_what: Japanese diplomatic pressure on the US is sustained at multiple levels.
insights.locator: From Japan’s side, there has been

insights.claim: A Japanese petition calling for withdrawal of the US sanctions on the ICC has received almost 175,000 signatures, and new university and civil society networks have formed in support of international justice.
insights.speaker: Simon Henderson
insights.so_what: Domestic public pressure in Japan raises the political cost of acquiescing to US policy.
insights.locator: Public opposition in Japan to the US

insights.claim: Henderson recommends Australia firmly denounce the US measures and express solidarity with the Japanese government and the Japanese nationals targeted.
insights.speaker: Simon Henderson
insights.so_what: A public break would mark a change in Australia's alliance posture toward the US.

insights.claim: Henderson recommends Australia coordinate with Japan and more vocal states, using international forums, to sustain political and diplomatic support for the ICC.
insights.speaker: Simon Henderson
insights.so_what: Points to a potential middle-power coalition on rule of law independent of Washington.

insights.claim: Henderson urges the Australian government to prevent US sanctions from being implemented in Australia and to publicly advise banks, financial institutions and other companies against excessive overcompliance.
insights.speaker: Simon Henderson
insights.so_what: Raises compliance-conflict risk for Australian banks caught between US secondary sanctions and domestic guidance.
insights.quote: Banks, financial institutions and other companies should be advised against excessive overcompliance

insights.claim: Henderson argues that dismantling the ICC would undermine the international rule of law, which is essential for global order and security.
insights.speaker: Simon Henderson
insights.so_what: Erosion of international legal institutions adds to a less predictable geopolitical backdrop.
insights.locator: The ICC is an independent and impartial body
